utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, may I introduce Kristina Belic, who is from New Jersey, USA, via Serbia, and has been assisting our team since the beginning of January. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, if I could quickly raise one matter that I have discussed with the Defence and that concerns Exhibit P6635, an intercept that was admitted in part, yesterday. That -- the document was truncated on the basis of an understanding that it contained a number of conversations not simply the one the witness alluded to, but a closer look reveals that there is only one conversation in that. I brought it to Mr. Robinson's attention. We reviewed it. We agree that the entirety of the -- 6635 should be admitted because for the same reason the portion was admitted. It's all one conversation. So I would ask the Court to have the Registry modify it accordingly with Mr. Reid's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that's one set of conversation between Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Kojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In which a number of people participate but it's the same conversation and indeed the earlier part of the conversation is alluded to in the latter part of the conversation, so it's another reason for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Do you confirm that, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be done. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Olmsted, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we have 65 ter 25900 on the screen. And if we could turn to page 31 of the English; page 22 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stanisic, on 17 January 1994, during your second term as RS MUP minister, you appointed Simo Drljaca assistant chief of CSB Banja Luka; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my signature on this decision but it does say in this decision -- I mean, it does say what you had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And this decision was issued under your name and that wouldn't have occurred without your authorisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Decisions are only signed by the minister, decisions on appointments.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 5 in both the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. President, I assume there's some technical delays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, there we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And on 27 April 1994, you appointed Mr. Drljaca to position of chief of SJB Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is not my signature. My signature is clear. You have it in documents. This is somebody on behalf of the minister. And I don't know when and I don't know who did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. But a person would not be appointed SJ -- or CJB chief without your authorisation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only give some clarification about what I knew. There was no CSB Prijedor at the time. There was a CSB Prijedor that was in the process of being established. Maybe it's somebody from the personnel department. Or maybe one of the under-secretaries. Maybe the under-secretary for public security sent him there to prepare facilities, to prepare everything that was needed in order to have the centre established.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To save time, I don't want you to speculate just focus on my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may these two pages be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6638, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we now have on the screen, D1076.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of us is a RS MUP administration for police duties and affairs report dated 3 August 1992. If we could turn to page 2 of both versions. I want to focus your attention, Mr. Stanisic, on the second paragraph in the B/C/S, which reports: "A special problem in certain areas is the paramilitary formations, groups and individuals that make war as they please. True, as I was informed, they were responding and helping the units of the Serbian army and police ..." Mr. Stanisic, my question is: You were aware, weren't you that in the early days of the conflict Serb paramilitary groups were responding to and helping the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I take a look at the date? May I see the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can turn to the first page but I'll tell you it's the 3rd of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it's not the beginning. It's the second half of 1992. Now we can go back to that page. While we're still on this, though, this document does not make any sense officially because there is no number. It could not have reached the minister's office. No report could have reached the minister's office without it being registered and logged. I don't see any number here. And I really cannot recall now. It was a long time ago. But I can try to help with this para unit as you had put it a moment ago, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, can you help by focussing on my question. My question is simply: You were aware that early on in the conflict paramilitary groups were helping and responding to the police and the army, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said yesterday as well that paramilitary groups came. They were brought in -- I mean, let me not be too extensive now. A member of the Presidency sent letters and brought them there. When they would first come they would report to the army. They would get a lot of weapons and then they'd become renegades. And here they say that they joined them sometimes. Usually when they'd be armed well, then they would become renegades from the army, and then they'd start doing other things as well so this group was expelled, I think, immediately in this period. As far as I can remember, Charlie's men, it was expelled in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have P3174 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you have the entire parts of this document in our evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour. I -- I assumed it's already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the last page of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. The -- I have a notation -- yes, here notation that end of this document is missing. So I wanted to see the signature part whether this was signed by the witness. But it's -- it seems missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And -- yes. And it was issued by the administration for police duties. It wasn't issued -- we're not purporting it was issued by Mr. Stanisic himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now if we could have P3174.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while that is coming up, Mr. Stanisic, let me put to you that the report we just looked at, the purpose of those reports were to inform you about events on the ground; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course reports that reach the minister have one purpose only; that is to say, to inform the minister about the part of the work that the minister has to be informed of. Not all reports end up on the minister's desk. There are a lot that end up at centres, stations, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. But this is a report from -- at the RS MUP level by the administration of police duties, and therefore they're preparing that report for you, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? The report that was on our screen a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's right. The 3 August report. That was prepared by your direct subordinates, the administration on police duties and in preparing that report, not for -- for the field, not for the SJBs, but for you, as minister.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Prosecutor. It would not have been serious, to put it mildly, if one of the assistants from the department for the police to send information to the minister without a number and without a signature. I really could not accept that. I claim that it is the obligation about the part of the work that the minister is supposed to know about, that is to say the general work of the Ministry of the Interior along general lines of work. The minister should be informed, and each and every such report arrives is recorded in the records of the minister's office and is assigned a number and also gets a number under which it is sent. How else could I take action if there is not a number and if there is no signature in terms of who had sent it. Perhaps somebody from the street had simply written this up to make a provocation. I cannot say. It's been a long time ago. And especially because it is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, in front of us we have a certificate issued by the SJB chief from Prijedor -- or, I'm sorry, from Pale who at the time was Malko Koroman, and it's a certificate concerning the issuing of a number of weapons to Vojo Vuckovic which we have evidence was the leader of the Yellow Wasps in Zvornik. Now, you were aware of the certificate, I'm not saying at the time, but you were aware of it, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, please let us clarify this. In this period of time, Malko Koroman had been relieved of his duties by the minister on the basis of a decision taken in May. It is true that he did not want to leave and you already know that from my case, and it is true that I have nothing to do with this. How could I have known about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's quickly look at P6386. Yes. Now, this is a cover page of a report submitted to you, the minister, and you will see that attached or enclosed with the report is a photocopy of a certificate from Pale SJB. Mr. Stanisic, that was the certificate that we just looked at that was issued by Malko Koroman; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I did not see any certificate, in terms of what you showed me a moment ago, but the content of this report that was sent to the minister, yes, I did see that. An action was taken on the basis of this report. The centre of security services started an investigation, and I don't know anything else about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Are --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But could I just add one more thing? I'm sorry. I replaced Malko Koroman by decision of mine in the month of May. He didn't want to leave the station. I sent Dragan Andan, an inspector, to carry out my decision. There was a rally there of over 10.000 people and we could not do that. We could not get that done. He didn't want to leave the police station. He created problems. But I never withdrew this decision on the basis of which I had relieved him of that duty as chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have 65 ter 25899 on the screen. I'm interested in page 3 of the English; page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stanisic, let me just repeat my question again: You were aware that Malko Koroman was providing weapons to members of the Yellow Wasps; correct? Please don't focus on the document, focus on my question, Mr. Stanisic. You were aware that the Yellow Wasps were receiving weapons from Malko Koroman; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And disciplinary proceedings were initiated and checks were carried out and the conclusion reached was that that was not correct. That is the information that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now we see on 18 January 1994, you appointed Mr. Koroman chief of the department for police duties in CSB Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, this is not my signature. And I know that he was appointed. So it wasn't I who appointed him. This was in the domain of the under-secretary for public security. But that is exactly when I was informed that there were disciplinary proceedings against him and that nothing had been established. And the proposal was that he be appointed again as chief -- I mean, that he stay on at the public security station in Pale. I did not allow that for him to be in that position as a single head of a single unit, so it was this organisational unit of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I do not understand, Mr. Stanisic, your explanation. You said: "I did not allow that for him to be in that position as a single head of single unit ..." Does it mean you didn't approve this appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the minister makes decisions on appointments at the proposal of the head of the organisational unit that wants to appoint a particular person and then the under-secretary for public security insisted that Malko Koroman since nothing had been established in the proceedings against him that a decision be made for him to stay on as chief of the public security station in Pale. I did not allow that for the following reason: I thought that he could not be the head of a separate organisational unit in the Ministry of the Interior. However, since nothing had been established, he could continue carrying out duties in a different unit where he would be under the control of his immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether or not you signed this document in front of you, it was you that appointed Mr. Koroman as the chief of the department for the police duties in Sarajevo CSB, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agreed that Malko Koroman, since nothing had been established, that's correct, that he should be assigned -- actually, since disciplinary proceedings had been carried out and nothing had been established then he would be assigned to a particular job but where he could not, I mean, hold the position of a person who organises work in an organisational unit, as he had been before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have page 4 of the English; page three of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Mr. Stanisic, I want to put to you -- no, I want to ask you a question before you look at the document, Mr. Stanisic, I want to put to you that, in fact, no disciplinary proceedings were initiated against Malko Koroman in 1992 or afterwards. That's what I put to you.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was informed, I was -- in charge of the proceedings. The proceedings were carried out at the centre of the security services in Sarajevo. They were in charge of the proceedings and I was informed the proceedings had been initiated and that they had taken place, and I left in 1992, and I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have in front of you is a 27 May 1994 decision issued under your name, under your authority, in which you appointed Mr. Koroman chief inspector of the police special operations in the office of the minister; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tendered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You've answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, please. May I explain? I'm saying that this is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand what you meant. But you approved it. Does it mean you didn't approve it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honour, I'm not aware of this decision. This was precisely at the time when we had clashed and when I was leaving and then in July I left the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you tendering two pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6637, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we may have on the screen, 65 ter 5290.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, what you have in front of you is an information from SJB Ilidza dated 5 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the second page. We can see at the top that this was submitted to the personal attention of you, the minister. Now, if we could go to page 5 of the English, page 6 of the B/C/S, we see that it reports that SSJB Ilidza delivered the following to the Serb volunteer and then provides a long list of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, other MUP officials were engaged in arming activities similar to those of Malko Koroman regarding paramilitaries. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These two documents that you mentioned don't have the same content. Your Honour, Ilidza is a municipality of the city of Sarajevo. At the police station -- on the premises of the police station, weapons were stocked of the entire military brigade as well as the weapons of the police in Ilidza. All that was stored there. This is probably a report to the effect that from that stockpile, they gave these weapons to the volunteers, because that was the most -- the safest depot. So the military weapons and the police weapons were stored there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we tendered this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6639, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have on the screen 65 ter 15476.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, you will agree that you signed this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And pursuant to this document, you note that the MUP issued Branislav Gavrilovic, also known as Brne, a Heckler, and a pistol, and you authorised him to carry those weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they informed me that the MUP had issued one Heckler to the said person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you knew that Branislav Gavrilovic was a commander of a SRS unit. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Branislav Gavrilovic, no. Branislav Gavrilovic was born in Sarajevo and he must have been engaged as a reservist and given weapons by the MUP at this point. Generally speaking, I never heard that Branislav Gavrilovic was part of the - what you did say? - SOS?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I said SRS, the Serbian Radical Party paramilitary volunteers. He was a member of those, Mr. Stanisic, I'll put to that you. And I'll ask you --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party, I'm not denying that. I understood you as saying "SOS." I don't know who belonged to whom. At this point he was probably engaged on some assignment and given the weapons, and these weapons were a Heckler and a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you -- you -- before issuing a certificate such as this you didn't do any background check to make sure you understood exactly who Branislav Gavrilovic was and why he needed these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I don't do the vetting. I don't run checks. This is a document that comes to my desk for my signature, and checks were supposed to be run by the organisational unit, if he was carrying out some assignment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6640, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you coming to a close?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer do you need to conclude?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just have a couple of more questions regarding paramilitaries, and I would really like to cover the issue of war crimes. I don't think that will take very long because my questions are quite limited and they are mainly asking him to confirm documents. And I just ask for the time to do that. And I apologise. I should have given a better estimate yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you haven't touched the issue of Koricanske Stijene at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I do have a few questions but if something has to go, that will have to go, but I would like -- ideally, I would like to ask questions about that. And, Your Honours, I really am trying to push this along as fast as I can. I learned some lessons yesterday with regard to this witness and the issue of time, and now I'm trying to rectify that and really hone in my questions. And I believe I can get through this fairly quickly, if you give me leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much time do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Realistically, Your Honours, 45 minutes, if I want to cover Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, please conclude in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, you were aware that paramilitaries in Zvornik were committing crimes against non-Serbs before the 11 July collegium meeting; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, sometime in the beginning of June, we knew about the incriminating activities of the Yellow Wasps in Zvornik. We didn't have full information, but I had just sent inspectors to inquire into that and to prepare the ground, as we call it, for arresting and eliminating that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you were aware, weren't you, that in June and July or -- I think it's more particular towards the end of June, maybe at some point in July, that ministers of the Bosnian Serb government were being stopped by the Yellow Wasps at check-points and vehicles -- Golf vehicles were being confiscated, and ministers, such as Mr. Ostojic, were being harassed. You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only ministers. They harassed the authorities and any passer-by, including ministers. That's what all these criminal groups do to achieve control and then commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, in fact, they stopped you at a check-point - isn't that correct? - in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I passed through one of their check-points, but we had knowledge from before that they were committing incriminating acts in the area where they were located. And I believe when I was setting out to that collegium meeting in Belgrade, I had personal experience that they were doing that, because they stopped me too. But we had knowledge about it before, and we had started an investigation to collect information in order to arrest that group. But when I set out to the collegium meeting on the 11th of July, I saw that for myself. Excuse me, if I may add one thing. Zvornik, all the way up to the month of June, was physically separated because there was only one road that you could pass through occasionally at a place called Sabati [phoen] because it was affected by constant conflict between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Army of Republika Srpska. It's only beginning with June that you could occasionally pass through escorted by a military convoy of tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because my question was simply whether you were stopped at this check-point and you have answered that. So let's move on to a different topic. Now, after a long trial and extensive evidence in your case before this Tribunal, the Trial Chamber found that when dealing with war crimes you focussed primarily on crimes committed against Serbs. That's what the Trial Chamber found; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't see my original judgement, but I maintain that this was not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have P2715 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, this is an order from you to the CSB chiefs. It's dated 16 May 1992. And if we could turn to page 3 of the English; page 2 of the B/C/S. We can see under section Roman numeral IV entitled "War crimes," you wrote: "Measures and activities conducted to document war crimes, these activities must involve collection of information and documents on war crimes against the Serbs." Mr. Stanisic, this was your first written order about the investigation of war crimes, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer without any explanation, Mr. Prosecutor. So if you allow me. The first sentence says --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Please just answer my first question. This was your first --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You issued -- you -- are you -- can you point us to an earlier order, written order by you, with regard to war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Could you repeat the question. I didn't understand you at all. This first question you asked, you want me to -- you want me to answer, and I had begun to answer, but I need to understand the question clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then let me repeat. I asked you whether this was your first written order concerning the investigation of war crimes, and I understand your answer to be "no." And so my follow-up question is: Can you point us to an earlier written order by you with regard to the investigation of war crimes because --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor should know, and I believe he knows, the difference between collecting documentation and investigation, and he should define the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not a proper intervention. But why don't you deal with it one by one? Whether the answer to the first question is no, please confirm that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, let's take this very simply. First of all, is it your assertion that this is not the first written order that you issued with regard to the investigation of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From day one, with insisted with the inner collegium that all crimes should be investigated, regardless of ethnicity, Serb or non-Serb. And if I may say, from this document, I cannot answer any question until we clarify what type of document this is and what it's about. Your Honour, if I may only ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I may ask my second question, Mr. Stanisic. My second question is: Can you point to us -- to an earlier order by you concerning investigation of war crimes? Can you point to an earlier document?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I off the cuff? I should have all the documentation before me if -- how can you ask me to do that from memory? This was 20 years ago. Give me a document and I'll comment on it. I insist, if you want me to make the right conclusion, to be allowed to comment on this document because you are misinterpreting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't feel the need for his comment. He has answered my questions. I'll leave it to you, if you want to pursue it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think his answer was fair enough. But why don't you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have 65 ter 18441 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, this is an order from you to the CSB chiefs dated 17 July 1992 and I want to draw your attention to the fourth paragraph. You write that it is necessary "to send copies of documents on mass atrocities against Serbs by armed and paramilitary Croat [sic] forces ..." Mr. Stanisic, did you issue this order?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just see the signature. There's no signature, but I know that a crime was committed in Sijekovac and this area, but we didn't have any information and we asked for information to be delivered. The crime was committed during the times of the former MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we wanted information about these atrocities that had been committed earlier, in the end of March, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I would like to intervene here with an objection. I think this line of questioning concerning interest of the republican authorities in prosecuting crimes against Serbs is not appropriate. Number one, it's not a particularly good use of time and you have been extremely generous to the Prosecution; but secondly, you precluded us throughout the trial from showing the crimes against the Serbs. And so if you allow the Prosecution to pursue this line, you're creating a very skewed record of concern over things that have never been able to be established. So in the combination of the fact that the Prosecution is way over their time, the very limited probative value of this, and the unfairness of one-sided evidence on -- of this nature, we would ask that it be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was waiting for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. During his direct examination, the witness took the position that the RS MUP was investigating war crimes regardless of who the perpetrators were or who the victims were, that they were doing their job fully, and I think he even used the words that the policy was clear and unambiguous. And that's the issue that I'm confronting. It's not the issue of whether, in fact, war crimes were committed against Serbs. That is not -- the -- --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Confronting the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm confronting the witness's evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But this is consistent with his evidence, as far as Serb victims are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As far as Serb victims are concerned. But, Your Honours, you will note that there is no mention here about non-Serb victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your questions should be directed whether he prosecuted non- -- non--- about the crimes committed against non-Serb victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the point of raising this issue? Just respond to Mr. Robinson's point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, we've heard in direct examination that its position that they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. You understand that we just -- we -- didn't -- didn't -- I'm sorry. We didn't allow the accused to expand on the issue of crimes committed against the Serbs. So could you respond to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll have to defer to -- I don't know the history of your case so I have to defer to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I would haven't risen but I thought that might be the nature of the problem that Mr. Robinson seemed to be alluding to something that happened in court that Mr. Olmsted was not familiar with. This is entirely a red herring. The Prosecution's case has not been that the exclusive focus on crimes against Serbs was put into question by the Prosecution because there were no crimes against Serbs. We never made that contention, and that's not the issue at all. The issue is whether or not there was an exclusive - or near exclusive - focus on crimes against Serbs, to the exclusion of crimes against Muslims. So the point that Mr. Robinson makes is entirely inapposite, and I don't think there should be confusion in the record as a result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Tieger. The Chamber agrees with you entirely. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we just turn to the last page on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, that's your signature; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6641, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 25916 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this is a dispatch from CSB Banja Luka to the SJBs, dated 14 December 1992, and Mr. Bulic announces a meeting of senior criminal investigation service officers from all centres will be held on 21 December at the RS MUP in Bijeljina. At this meeting: "The process of documenting crimes, war crimes against the Serbian civilian population, the crime of genocide, and the war crimes of destroying Orthodox cemeteries, churches, and other cultural and historical monuments will be analysed." Mr. Stanisic, the focus of this meeting and the focus of the operative work of your crime inspectors was on crimes committed against Serbs and not against crimes committed by non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, please. I don't know about this document. I'm not aware of it because it was not in the purview of the minister in his office. But your claim that only crimes against Serbs were investigated is not true. Crimes against the entire population of Republika Srpska were investigated. You're putting questions to me, taking things out of context. We did investigate all crimes, including against Serbs because that's our job, against both Serbs and Muslims. And you are only showing me documents that refer to crimes against Serbs, but they are not the only documents. That was one part of our work, especially because there was a problem with crimes against Serbs in the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina where the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina was active, and they carried victims in, in their arms, and nobody carried out the on-site investigation. There was no on-site investigation. Only fear remained about the crimes. You take certain things out of context, and then I get a question that I cannot answer in a way that -- that would assist getting to the truth before this Court. It's true, both crimes against Serbs and non-Serbs were investigated. It would be more appropriate to show me the statistics of 1992 as to how many criminal reports were filed concerning crimes against Serbs and concerning crimes against Muslims. That would give us an authentic picture, especially since the -- there were crimes that were dealt with by the MUP and crimes dealt with by the military security. We should see the statistics concerning the MUP and the crimes that concerned the MUP. I'm sorry, Your Honours, for taking time, but I really tried to clarify things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let me clarify one thing you said. Your crime inspectors were not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer the question. Mr. Stanisic, did you present that statistics in your trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, back to you, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This part of the question refers to an entirely other segment of crimes against the Serbs in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina where on-site investigations were not carried out and still the families brought in victims. So we tried to see how we could do some sort of an investigation to leave a trace of the crimes that were committed. And now it is being portrayed as only crimes against the Serbs were investigated, which is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Stanisic, if I can put to you this. It is not, in fact, the case that you offered statistics on a number of cases that -- number of case of war crimes committed against non-Serbs that your RS MUP investigated in 1992 and, in fact, the statistics would be negligible on that number?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, but there was also a negligible number of criminal reports that were filed for crimes against the Serbs. There was no distinction made when it came to crimes in the entire territory of Republika Srpska and still it would have been only logical because there's a higher percentage of Serbians living in Republika Srpska so the number of crimes should have been higher and the number of investigations should have been higher. But the conditions were really difficult. One could not work well. We only did as much as we could, given the conditions that prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6642, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 25913 on the screen. Now, this is an activity report from CSB Sarajevo dated 6 October 1992. And if we can have -- keep it on page 1 for the English but go to page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stanisic, I want to draw your attention to the -- well, it's the second full paragraph of this report which reports that seven criminal reports --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, please. Let's go back to the first page. I want to see who the author of the document is. And I also want to see the last page with the signature block, to see who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn to the --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And now the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And Mr. Tusevljak testified in your case as a Defence witness, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say something about the document. The document was not sent to the minister. Please. It was sent to the chief of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Stanisic, wait for the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question simply is that Mr. Tusevljak, who signed this document, was called by you in your case; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now let's focus on the paragraph that I want to draw your attention which is the second full paragraph. It says that seven criminal reports have already been submitted to competent prosecutor's office against 33 persons for whom there are grounds to suspect they have committed crimes of genocide against the Serbian people. Mr. Stanisic, this is your crime police executing your orders to focus on war crimes committed against the Serb population; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done by the service which elucidated all crimes. In this particular case, the crime was committed against the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do we find that passage?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's towards the bottom of the page. Starts with: "Documenting crimes of genocide and war crimes against the Serbian people," and continues from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6643, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Koricanske Stijene. Let's bring up on the screen D1883.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stanisic, we heard your evidence on direct examination. Now what's in front of you is a letter from the Banja Luka prosecutor to CSB Banja Luka dated 30 September 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I can read.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, and this is with regard to the Koricanske Stijene case that's already in evidence in this case. And we see that the prosecutor is returning the case file to the police to identify and arrest the perpetrators. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And under the criminal procedures that existed at the time, it was the duty of the police to identify the perpetrators and to file a criminal report against known perpetrators; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And until --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they managed to establish who the perpetrators are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And until that criminal report is filed against known perpetrators, the prosecutor could not request that the criminal investigation by an investigative judge be initiated; correct? That was the procedures that existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Ministry of the Interior does not assess the quality of evidence at hand. It is also not authorised to qualify a crime. It is the prosecutor who does that. Our obligation was to gather information and to file a criminal report or an official report to forward that information to the prosecutor or to the court and then the prosecutor qualifies the crime -- the crime and asks for additional information to corroborate the evidence at hand. So this, from then on, is within his purview, as well as his co-operation with the authorised organ of the Ministry of the Interior that operates in the territory of that particular court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's return to my question. Until the prosecutor receives a criminal report against known perpetrators, the prosecutor is not in a position to send a formal request to the court for an investigative judge to initiate a criminal investigation - isn't that correct? - under the criminal procedures codes that existed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. The Ministry of the Interior submits information about the grounds to suspect that somebody perpetrated a crime and the prosecutor corroborates that suspicion. So the prosecutor has the right to ask for additional information, and up to then enough information was submitted to the public prosecutor to tell him who the possible suspects are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me see if I can ask it one last time. Mr. Stanisic, in order for an investigative judge to begin a criminal investigation, there has to be a criminal report against identified perpetrators; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There could be an official report or any sort of information, because the prosecutor was in charge of investigations. It could be citizens to provide him with information. It didn't have to be the MUP. It could be ordinary citizens, and if the prosecutor received such information -- information, they had to proceed with investigation using the help of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Last document. 1D4537 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while this is coming up, Mr. Stanisic, let me ask you: Did Mr. Karadzic or any member of the RS Presidency ever tell you that four of the perpetrators of the Koricanske massacre were, in fact, identified; that they knew the names of them?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. Maybe you have something that will jog my memory. I don't remember that Karadzic ever told me any such thing. Give me something. Give me something to jog my memory. As things stand at the moment, I don't remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But you knew that members of the police, of your police, committed that crime. You knew this in 1992, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information that was available was submitted to the prosecutor, and he proceeded in that case. The fact is that everything --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question is quite simple --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to remind the witness if he -- if he so wishes, you may invoke your right pursuant to Rule 90(E) at this time. Because you did so when asked by Mr. Karadzic. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, in 1992, you knew that members of your police had committed the killings, the massacre at Koricanske Stijene; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I was informed about the incident. I sent instructions as to what needed to be done, what measures needed to be taken by the Ministry of the Interior. The Ministry of the Interior acted on my order. They secured the evidence. They -- they made sure that witnesses were available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Stanisic. The question was whether you knew that members of the police had committed the killings. Could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at that moment, I didn't know that the perpetrators were police members. To this very day, Your Honours, when it comes to the perpetrators of that crime, and this has been investigated here and established here, I claim that people who committed that crime were members of the intervention platoon from the military police of the Prijedor intervention platoon, and they had police members as their escorts. But according to what I know, the police escorts were not involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Given the time, Mr. Olmsted, we'll allow you to deal with this document before concluding your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn -- first of all, you can see from the first page, Mr. Stanisic, that this is a letter from CJB Banja Luka to Banja Luka district prosecutor's office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- just a second. It is probably CSB not CJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, actually -- well, if I could give a little bit of history. At a certain point in time they became CJBs rather than CSBs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now we can see from the subject heading, Mr. Stanisic, that this letter pertains to the Koricanske Stijene case; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably CJB at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'm just drawing your attention to the subject matter heading which says Koricanske Stijene report on collecting the necessary information. You see that, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2 of the English. We'll stay where we are on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, I want you to look at the third paragraph. The third paragraph states: "We also hereby inform you that by checking the protocol books we have determined that the request of the Banja Luka ... prosecutor's office ... of 30 September 1992," that's the document we just looked at, "has been received by the centre, but action was not taken in accordance with it, nor was any report on collecting the necessary information submitted to the Banja Luka public prosecutor's office." Mr. Stanisic, my question is: The police never took any action in response to the prosecutor's request for the police to gather additional information about the perpetrators; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. This was drafted in 1999; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police informed the prosecutor that the perpetrators were currently members of the military, and they were on military missions. It was the prosecutor's obligation to approach the military security and to bring those people in. The police couldn't do that if the perpetrators were members of the army. That had to be done by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But, Mr. Stanisic, you'll agree that that is not what this document says. This document says the police never provided any additional information about this case in response to the prosecutor's 30th September 1992 letter, and that was in fact the case, wasn't it, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if I remembered it well from my case, the prosecutor who was in charge of the case did testify, and said that the police co-operated with him at the time when that was within the purview of the police. You were here. I don't have that information because the prosecution took the case over but I am telling you what the prosecutor in charge of the case stated during my case. I can't say anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stanisic, I put to that you that that is not, in fact, what that witness said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're tendering this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I may have one last question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Given what you knew about the activities of the CSB Banja Luka and SJB Prijedor, particularly with regard to the -- the detention facilities and non-Serb detainees, you were aware that your two-sentence dispatch from the 31st of August, 1992, would have had no impact whatsoever on that investigation, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I will need to object now and then. Ask Your Honours to compel the witness to testify -- to -- to give this answer to this question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Stanisic, you agree to invoke your right pursuant to Rule 90(E)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. For the same reason that we compelled you to answer the question in your examination-in-chief, we also compel you to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question is this: Given what you knew about the activities of CSB Banja Luka and SJB Prijedor, particularly with regard to non-Serb detainees held in these unofficial detention facilities, you were aware that your two-sentenced dispatch from 31 August 1992 concerning the Koricanske Stijene incident would have no impact whatsoever on the investigation of that case; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is not correct that I could do anything else at that moment. I issued an order within my remit. The order was acted on. The case was handed over to the prosecutor. It is correct that I couldn't follow the matter through because I was dismissed from my position, but while I was in office, all the actions were taken. I handed over the case to the prosecutor. The prosecutor took the case. And then I left and I could no longer have any influence on the course of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this may be admitted into evidence. And that concludes my cross-examination and let me express my gratitude to the Trial Chamber for being -- allowing me to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6644, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, in view of the time that you gave to the Prosecutor and the topics that he dealt with, of course I have questions, quite a few of them, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed. If you wish, we can take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. We may start the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at seven to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies, good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Minister.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are again speaking Serbian so I kindly ask you to pause after my questions. I'll start with very short questions, I'm hoping for short answers, and I'll start with last things first. On page 32 of today's record, you spoke about the crime that was committed at Koricanske Stijene. Could you please tell us how many professional policemen, if any, were among the perpetrators of the crime?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None. I just said, they were members of the intervention platoon, and they were all members of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 28 of today's transcript, the Prosecutor put it to you that the prosecutor couldn't do anything before he received a criminal report. How often were criminal reports filed, if at all, if the perpetrator was unknown, an NN perpetrator, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prosecutor acted on the information received from the Ministry of the Interior. Most of the time, the perpetrators were unknown because the ministry was duty-bound to register every incident and inform the prosecutor's office about it and also to file a written information, irrespective of whether the identity of the perpetrators was known or unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could we please display P6643 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us which CSB this is? And what region did it cover?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can see from the document, this is the Security Services Centre of Romanija and Birac region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What territory could this CSB access to carry out complete investigations; and what about the crimes that happened in the territories to which it didn't have access?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. Could you please be more specific or could you rephrase?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The question was a bit confusing, I admit. Which territories did this CSB have access to, and, thus, carry out complete investigations; and which territories could it -- it could not access?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that initially, up to the month of July, it was impossible or virtually impossible to move from the place where you were, and the reason for that was combat that was ongoing and communications were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, this centre, what could they do in respect of crimes committed against Serbs in the city of Sarajevo itself that was under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They couldn't do anything in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So then what does documentation mean or, rather, collecting information about crimes against Serbs? To what extent do they collect evidence and to what extent do they carry out investigations?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre of security services carries out its work in the territory where it functions, together with its members, and that is where they carry out investigations and everything else as envisaged by the law on the basis of which they operate. Now, as far as crimes against Serbs are concerned, those committed in Sarajevo and elsewhere - there were many - they could only collect information from the families of the victims who managed to get out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 15 of today's transcript, it was stated that the late-Minister Ostojic had been abused, that you were stopped, et cetera. Can you tell us what the reason was for the Yellow Wasps to turn against the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I cannot speak specifically about all of their motives. But in terms of what we know, first of all, they wanted to take the area, even physically, to create pre-conditions for themselves, and then they carry out these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why were they not courteous to the authorities? On page 15 or 16, you said that you had already initiated proceedings. What was the reason? Did they know that you had started these proceedings? Was that wise? Wasn't it wiser for them to be courteous?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. As soon as conditions were created and as soon as we found out, I personally sent people to collect documentation, how many of them there were there and how many weapons they had, and so on and so forth. So all of these tactical measures, in order to prepare this work so that at a given point in time when conditions are created and when reinforcements arrive from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, this could be eliminated because, at that moment, we did not have available forces in Zvornik, in order to have such forces resolve that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what were the crimes for which they were arrested and eliminated as a unit?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were arrested, it was the military security and members of the Ministry of the Interior that took part in their arrest, and they were reinforced with this detachment from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That is how this group was divided. There were a great many of them. According to the information that I received that was compiled after the arrest, military security took Vuckovic, Repic - I think that was the name - and there was a suspicion that he had committed war crimes in Zvornik, I think against 200 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the ethnicity of the victims?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The victims were of Muslim ethnicity and the mentioned person was of Serb ethnicity. As a matter of fact, he was a citizen of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I think he was from Sabac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they indicted and convicted because they stopped Minister Ostojic and you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no way. You see that that's not even mentioned at all in the notes and in the reports of the crime police and the military security that dealt with this other part. There is no mention of any ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 10 of today's transcript, I'm afraid that the word that you used "inokosan [phoen]" for Malko Koroman was not precisely translated as being a single head of a particular organisation. Why would somebody be eligible to work in one body where he would not be the single person in charge or in another body where he would be the single person in charge?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it depends on the quality of the person involved and jobs are allocated on that basis. And the assessment was that Malko Koroman, and it was Alija Delimustafic who appointed him chief before the war in Pale, and in May my assessment was that could not do this job properly. Of course, to the best of my knowledge, when I left in 1992, the disciplinary commission interviewed him, I mean, they did their work, and it was established that there were no incriminations involved and then he was allocated a job on the basis of his quality. So he was removed from a position where he could broadly exercise influence over what that organ -- done. Rather, he was given a job where he had specific tasks and he was the only person who was responsible for carrying out those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 13, a document from the 11th of April, 1992, was shown to you and it has to with Brne. On the 11th of April, 1992, did we have criminal records in respect of this Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any records whatsoever and you can see on the basis of our reports that it was stated that that is precisely the greatest reason for making our work so difficult in terms of carrying out a selection in order to make an assessment as to which persons were prone to what kind of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that persons first volunteered and then became renegades; paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2302, could we have a look at that now. Yes, there is a translation. This has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on the 9th of July, the war board of commissioners of Ilidza is saying that the use of the motel is being approved to them as a volunteer unit, and down here it says that: "The commander, Branislav Gavrilovic, will be conducting admission and training of Serbian volunteers arriving to this area." Is this something that was not allowed on the basis of the law? Is this acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The law, even in the former Yugoslavia, and then also our own regulations say, there was this category of volunteers. I mean, first in the JNA and then later on in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the transcript, yet again, but it is a question of double negation. It doesn't exist in English. So was this allowed on the basis of the law?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on, since there was this lack of control, did you take any measures in respect of these volunteers and other individuals that got out of control?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that all paramilitary groups that appeared were arrested during 1992 and expelled from the territory of Republika Srpska. And we did not do that -- I mean, it wasn't only we as Ministry of the Interior that did that. Those who were renegades, those who had nothing do with the military, and then the army dealt with those who came to them as volunteers and became renegades as well, and they still had the status of members of the army. Then the army dealt with them and expelled them. Now to what extent, I don't know. It was really up to them. I do know, I do know seriously, that they did deal with that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown D1076.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of August, were you still minister?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, could you focus on this. So it is the administration for police duties and affairs that is sending you a report; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the realisation of your order?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says: Report on the realisation of the order strictly confidential, et cetera. That is my order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page now. I believe it should be the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here: "Acting in accordance with your order, I visited most stations." Now would you focus on this paragraph: "I insisted with the chief of the public security station Ilidza that the problem of so-called Brnetovci [phoen], Brne's men, and Chetniks from the detachment Dusan Silni who were staying in the orchard at Rakovica should be solved in agreement with the army command."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "These units have around 100 members. They are well armed and act independently. Although according to the chief of the SJB Ilidza they have not been making any problems, I still insisted in accordance with your order that their status be resolved in agreement with the Serb army so that they should either be put under the single command or they should leave the area of Ilidza." Was this in accordance with your order?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you say how this developed further, the relationship between them and the army? Did the state security provide information as to ...

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I cannot remember all the details now, but I know that all para units that were in the territory of Republika Srpska were subjected to expulsions, arrests, expulsions from the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2305, could that document please be shown to the witness now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before we go -- You just saw this document from Sarajevo - what is it? - administration for police tasks. Now you agree -- agree with the authenticity of this document? Shall we upload it again, D1076.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I spoke about the content of the document. I mean, I answered the questions put by Mr. Karadzic. I think that this document was before us a short while ago, when the Prosecutor was putting his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is page 2, but the document is dated the 3rd of August, 1992, and also it refers to the number of your order.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I saw it when you showed it to me. But you just read out a paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the first page of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It has an ERN number. And you see the heading here where it says: Report on the realisation of the order strictly confidential, et cetera. Acting on your order, was that your order?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my order --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The answer is the 3rd of August; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That means that the chief of centre -- no, of this department for police affairs did act on the basis of my order, and he did compile this report. And I see it says here "submit to the Ministry of the Interior, to the minister."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree that you received this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember now whether I received it. But, yes, certainly it is a report on the basis of my order, because I sent this order, and that is how I identify this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in answering the question from Mr. Olmsted, you stated: Perhaps somebody from the street had simply written this, I cannot say. Do you stand by it, that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said that. Because there was no number up there and there was no signature. Well, now, too. I mean, I claim that this is my order. I mean, what Mr. Karadzic asked me about, I didn't see that before because we were focussed on one paragraph that the Prosecutor showed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I claim now, too, it doesn't have a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. P2305 now, please. And then page 2 immediately so that we could see who it was that sent this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who this person is who sent it, Minister?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Srdjan Sehovac. He was the commander, I think, at the Novo Sarajevo police station, if I remember correctly. And I think I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 1 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that he worked for national security?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, there were two persons named Sehovac: One was Srdjan, the other one was Goran. Goran was commander of the station in Novo Sarajevo, and Srdjan worked in national security. I'm sorry about this mistake. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's an Official Note from him and the first paragraph says it relates to Brne's men. And then he says in the second paragraph with the arrival of the new commander, Colonel Spasoje Cajic, Brne's formation felt that it would no longer have the privileges it used to have. And then it says further on: "It should be emphasised that the civilian authorities and employees of the MUP are in their way because they slander them as thieves and criminals," et cetera. Tell me, was there any love lost between the official authorities, including the police, and these Brne's men?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We object because it's leading. This is certainly not an issue that is covered by his line of questioning thus far, and Mr. Karadzic should have presented a question before directing this witness to this particular passage and ask for him to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. But it is related to the issue of the point raised with respect to Gavrilovic. Do you follow -- did you follow the point of Mr. Olmsted, Mr. Karadzic? Please reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. I apologise. I will do so now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, from the -- from the month of April until this date here, in February, what was the evolution of the attitude to this unit?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the units -- all the criminal groups, rather, that came to Republika Srpska, the rule was that, first of all, they would create a territory for themselves and attack the police and the authorities who tried to prevent them. It says here that they are manoeuvring to create their own space, and this official is reporting about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, on page 84, you were quoted as saying, "They took thieves and criminals ..." Can you tell me, did the Serbian Radical Party nominate people who were not criminals to positions that belonged to the Serbs in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was talk about two different things. I was talking about members who were bent on crime, and they existed from the times of the former regime. They were activated as reservists. Under the aegis of the former Ministry of the Interior, they were called up because not enough non-Serbs responded to call-ups to the JNA. I don't know what kind of influence the SDS could have had. Anything I would say would be speculation.
