utterances.text: Would you like that add anything, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I understand the Defence's point. But presenting information this way, by reading a long passage and then asking the witness to comment on it is, you know, not only not helpful but I believe is leading. It's directing him to provide a specific type of answer, to confirm Mr. Karadzic's point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is not of the view that it was -- it was leading. We agree with Mr. Robinson's observation. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you answer, Mr. Minister.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood this to be your position, that agreements should be strictly adhered to, meaning the agreements on distributing senior positions in the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From what you know, did the Serb side honour these agreements or did it impose its own staff on Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be unfair to say that. The broad -- the -- the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina is very wide, but, for instance, in the SUP of the city of Sarajevo where I worked, the Serb side honoured everything. I know, however, there were some problems from the second side and even the third side, but the HDZ was responsible for a smaller amount of these problems than the SDA.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 5 in Serbian and 6 in English. Next page in English, and next page in Serbian. The English page should be 5 but I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this paragraph where I say, We did not impose a single Muslim. And I say, Muslim cadres should be appointed by the Muslim party that represents the people. Tell me, did we impose anyone on them? How is it consistent with your experience, as far as our conduct is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just tell you the general position was to adhere strictly to the agreement on dividing up senior executive positions. And I cannot speak specifically about this, but I see what's written, and this confirms that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a lot more, but we tender the entire document. I won't spend more time on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4287, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that I dealt with these things not with you but Mr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we show 65 ter 32006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What are these?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my conversation with Mr. Zepinic in November 1991. He was number one on the Serbian side in the police, in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I -- I meant to ask you to put your question first before putting the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's certainly not on the first page, Mr. Minister. How did I resolve these misunderstandings with Mr. Zepinic, and did Zepinic do his duty?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that you were in contact with him, but I also know - and we've seen from earlier texts - that Zepinic did not make enough of an effort for appointments to be made within the framework of the agreement, and I know you had words with him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 3 in Serbian and page 2 in English. In English, it's the last paragraph at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He tells me that we stand better in the city. That's where you were the chief; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I say here: "Hell, you'll see when all these things come to the surface what the MUP is doing." Distributed Muslim -- weapons to the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters need a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. And it's probably straddling the next page, too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, what is the date of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 20th November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is approximately what the situation was like. As I've said several times here, reserve members of the army were not allowed to join the Yugoslav People's Army, instead they were called up as reservists into the police, and lots of things happened. I was still in the SUP of the city, but they could not control that segment anymore. The minister was in charge, and there was a special advisor to the minister for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4288, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, did the MUP provide political parties with information about illegal activities in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? From where I was sitting, I didn't provide any information to any political parties. I don't know if anybody did that from other offices. I don't know. You have to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the MUP inform the president of the assembly, the president of the Presidency, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, you mean state authorities? Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show 1D00042.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before uploading the document, could you ask the witness some more specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was: Whether we had the opportunity to find out about illegal doings, wrong-doings in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, the State Security Service which was mostly involved in collecting intelligence was controlled by the SDA and the HDZ. We saw that when this post of deputy chief that belonged to Serbs was abolished. And, as far as the Serb side is concerned, even if some reports reached them, it was very terse. They probably informed their own people in a much more satisfactory manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tendered this document. English page 5, Serbian page 6. First of all, this is the secretary of President Milosevic followed by Mr. Milosevic himself. And the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure we have looked -- looked at this document at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's referring to the document that had been left on the screen that has already having been tendered. He hasn't gotten to the point to tender this one yet. He just asked his general question about this topic and now he's going to show the pertinent section of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh. Yes, I understood. Page 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the Serbian page two pages further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm talking to President Milosevic here and I tell him we received some material, showing that their people were doing illegal things, distributing weapon, calling up reservists, creating an army. I'm just informing him for the sake of Kadijevic who should know what is afoot in Bosnia. Were they indeed creating their own army and did the Muslim part of the MUP participate in the creation of that army?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior then had in its hands certain information. I believe in July 1991 in the hall of the police, in the area of the city SUP where I worked, a meeting of the Main Board of the SDA was held and, among other things, they decided - and I forgot to say the meeting was attended by the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the president of the SDA - they decided to establish a military wing of the SDA and the head of that staff was supposed to be Mr. Izetbegovic. For us, it was terrible news that the head of state should head the staff of some paramilitary organisation that was being established in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That really caused a lot of fear and confusion. We didn't know what to do next. How could then, for instance, the ministry receive an order from that head of state, knowing what we already knew at that time about Mr. Izetbegovic? And, in that context, I suppose, you are having this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To make things clear, which Kadijevic do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Kadijevic was, at that time, called minister of national defence. Or was it called secretary at the time? Secretary of national defence of the federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tendered this document, to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI, D4289, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I won't spend any more time, although have I many more documents. I'll tender them from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Stanisic. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your testimony. Also, I'd like to thank Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for his co-operation and assistance. You may be excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Our thanks also go to you, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the next witness is ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next witness is Mr. Orlovic, and he'll -- he's ready to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before we hear his evidence, shall we go into private session briefly in order to deal with a couple of matters.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Orlovic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Orlovic.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. How are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for asking. I'm fine. I would kindly ask you to pause between my questions and your answers and speak slowly so that all of your sentences may be properly recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Orlovic, did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D9666.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the first page of your statement in Serbian and in English before you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're starting your answers too quickly, so please make a pause. Did you read the statement and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page so that he may be able to identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately reflect what you stated? Is there anything that you need to correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions today to you in the courtroom as the ones you were asked when your statement was taken, would your answers, in essence, be the same as in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO ORLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm tendering this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objections, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President. Only to note that the statement contains a number of leading questions which should go to the weight of the evidence in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4294, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I'm going to read a short summary of Mr. Mihajlo Orlovic's statement in English. [In English] Mihajlo Orlovic worked as a journalist at the RS Radio and Television in Banja Luka. Before the conflict broke out in BH, he worked at the Sanski Most Radio. He was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia in the former SFRY, but after the breakup of the SFRY, he did not join any party. The SDA was formed in Sanski Most a few days before the SDS. Ethnic tensions began to rise during the conflict in Croatia and this spread great fear among Serbs, who were afraid that the killings carried out during the Second World War could repeat again. The first incidents in the territory of Sanski Most municipality were caused by Muslims, and during one of these incidents, a soldier was killed. After these frequent provocations, the Crisis Staff ordered that an appeal be broadcast to all citizens to surrender illegal fire-arms and military equipment which the inhabitants of some Bosnian Muslim neighbourhoods and villages ignored. As a consequence, women and children and old people were called on to come out of their homes so that the legal civilian and military police forces could conduct a search and confiscate the weapons. During the search, those people found in possession of illegal arms were taken into custody, while the peaceful citizens who did not endanger others could feel at ease regardless of their affiliations. All peace-loving citizens sought protection in schools and halls, and efforts were made to enable them to do that. Those Muslim extremists who did not want to surrender their weaponry resisted and put up a fight. Seven Serbian soldiers were killed in the clashes. Numerous attempts were made to establish peace and the rule of law and order in the municipality. For instance, the Serbs offered the Muslims in Sanski Most to divide the territory in which they operated politically. Furthermore, negotiations were conducted with the representatives of the Muslim side and appeals were broadcast on the radio for the calming of tensions. Radio Sanski Most tried to be up to date and to report objectively about the situation, while insisting on the preservation of peace. On 25th of March, 1992, all Serb territories in the municipality were declared part of the Bosnian Serb republic as a unified Serb municipality of Sanski Most and on the 3rd of April, 1992, the municipality became part of the ARK. The Serbs established authorities in Sanski Most on 11th of April, 1992. They wanted to remain in the joint state. Most people welcomed these decisions with relief, although they saw it as a temporary solution and expected that an agreement on joint participation in the authorities would soon be reached. The Muslim part of the police station which did not want to remain part of the Serbian police force broke away and set up its own police force in the premises of the municipal assembly building. The Serbian authorities called on them to return their weapons and leave the building, but since they did not comply, it was decided to disarm them. No one was wounded or killed during this operation. At the beginning of the conflict and until the authorities in Sanski Most brought everything under control, individuals and criminal groups exploited the situation of chaos for their own benefits. For general safety reasons, the authorities had to introduce a curfew and controls on movement that applied to all citizens. For a certain time, all telecommunications and road connections were cut, and all decisions were made in the SDS Municipal Board and in the Municipal Assembly but for the benefit of all citizens of Sanski Most. At the same time, the SDA used various instruments of propaganda aimed at causing chaos and disorders. Many citizens of all ethnicities decided to leave Sanski Most municipality because of the war-time poverty and personal insecurity. Convoys of civilians were organised and escorted by the Serb civilian and military police in order to ensure them a safe passage. At the same time, columns of Serbs were arriving from the places where Muslims and Croats were in power. All citizens who wanted to leave could maintain, sell, or exchange their property. On June the 13th, 1992, the Sanski Most Crisis Staff adopted a decision to stop the looting of private property by arresting and detaining the perpetrators and seizing the stolen property. In many cases, Serb refugees were accommodated into abandoned houses temporarily. Nevertheless, several thousand Muslims decided to remain and continued to live in Sanski Most until the end of the conflict in 1995. And that is a short summary. At that moment, I do not have questions for Mr. Orlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Orlovic, as you have noted, your evidence in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing. That is, through your written witness statement in lieu of your oral testimony. We'll adjourn for today, and tomorrow you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Orlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of February, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.
